messages.mes:
*Cool wind moves through the rough grass around Alaric Red's boots.*

*The last thing that belongs to Earth is still there in memory—an old life, a world without visible mana, Classes, or this impossible second beginning. The present is different: the smell of soil and distant woodsmoke, an unfamiliar sky, and stone walls beyond the public road.*

*Alaric Red is already standing on an uncultivated roadside verge outside the nearby city. Cultivated fields and fenced holdings begin farther away. No one is close enough to have witnessed the instant of arrival.*

*The body is Human, healthy, and eighteen years old. Simple traveler's clothes are already being worn; a small pouch holding five silver rests at the belt. The memories are still from Earth.*

*A translucent interface opens across Alaric Red's vision.*

`SYSTEM INITIALIZATION COMPLETE`
`Origin: Earth`
`World: Avereth`
`Race: Human`
`Age: 18`
`Level: 1 | Rank: F`

`BASE STATS`
`STR 5 | VIT 5 | AGI 5 | INT 5 | PER 5 | WIL 5`

`Location: Public roadside verge outside Alderwatch, Valedorn Crown`
`Arrival Witnesses: NONE`
`Starting Possessions: Simple Traveler's Clothes | Small Pouch | 5 Silver`
`Local Common Language: Integrated`
`Mandatory Quest: NONE`

`CHARACTER CREATION — STEP 1/2`
`Choose your Base Class:`

`Warrior   — Favored Stats: STR / VIT`
`Mage      — Favored Stats: INT / WIL`
`Guardian  — Favored Stats: VIT / WIL`
`Duelist   — Favored Stats: STR / AGI`
`Ranger    — Favored Stats: AGI / PER`

`Your chosen Class immediately applies +1 to both Favored Stats at Level 1.`
`After choosing a Class, select exactly 2 Skills from that Class's Base Skill Pool.`

`Reply with your Class choice.`

*The System waits. Story time does not move during Character Creation.*

messages.mes:
The road took him through fields still wet with morning, cart ruts hard from yesterday's sun. Ahead the walls grew slowly, grey stone patched with older masonry, and the gates admitted a short line of traffic: farmers with handcarts, a drover prodding two geese ahead of him, a woman leading a mule loaded with firewood. Nobody looked twice at a young man on foot in plain clothes.

Inside, Alderwatch smelled of bread and horse dung and woodsmoke. The main street ran downhill from the gate between timber-framed fronts, awnings cranked out over barrels and baskets, a smith's hammer already ringing somewhere off to the left. A boy swept a doorstep and stepped aside as Alaric passed. He asked the way once, at a stall where a woman was selling early apples, and she pointed with her chin up a side lane: "Guild? Left at the well, the big door with the crossed spears."

The hall stood where she said, larger than most of the street around it, a stone front with a wide arched door and a painted sign of crossed spears above it. The door stood open. Warm air came out carrying ink, lamp oil and the noise of a morning crowd — boots on boards, low talk, the scratch of a quill somewhere near the front.

Inside, a long counter ran along the left wall behind which clerks worked, and a large notice board dominated the far wall, papered with contract slips in several colors. A few adventurers stood reading it: a broad woman in mail with a shield slung at her back, a wiry pair in hunting leathers. A short clerk with ink-stained fingers glanced up from the counter as Alaric came in, and waited to see if he wanted anything.

messages.mes:
"Red. Right." The clerk pulled a ledger across the counter and wet his quill on a stone without looking up. "Alaric — spelling?"

He wrote it as Alaric said it, the quill scratching in a quick, practiced hand, then set the quill down and looked at him properly. Young, clean, no visible scars, a staff slung on his back. The clerk had seen enough new faces that morning to sort them without much thought.

"Registration's a one-time fee. Two silver. That covers your entry in the rolls, your Guild slip, and your rank — you'd start at Novice, same as everyone does." He tapped the ledger. "Separate thing from what you can do, mind. The Guild writes down your rank, it doesn't give it to you. There's a measuring stone for that, if you care to know your standing. Most do."

Behind Alaric the shield-wearing woman finished reading the board and went out, boots thudding on the boards.

"So. Two silver and a signature, and you're in the rolls. You can take contracts the same day — Novice work only at first, the slips marked for it. Payment's posted on each one and it's guaranteed at the counter; you bring the proof back here and we settle it." He turned the ledger toward Alaric and pushed a stub of charcoal across with it.

"That's the whole of it. Want to go ahead?"

messages.mes:
The clerk swept the two silver off the counter, bit one out of habit, and dropped both into a lockbox under the ledger. "Sign there."

The charcoal dragged rough across the page. The clerk turned the book back, read the name, and reached along the counter to a shelf where a small wooden tray sat full of thin metal plates. He chose one, tapped it twice against the wood, and the metal rippled faintly, words rising in its surface.

"Your plate. It's keyed to you — shows your Guild standing when a clerk reads it, and it's how we know whose proof is whose when you bring work in. Lose it, it costs to replace, so don't." He set it on the counter. "Now the stone, if you want your measure."

It stood against the wall past the end of the counter, a waist-high block of pale crystal, its surface worn dull by years of palms. Alaric laid his hand on it at the clerk's nod. The crystal warmed under his fingers and a faint blue glow climbed inside it, steady and shallow, and settled.

"Rank F," the clerk said, reading the depth of the light the way other men read weather. "Bottom rung, same as everyone starts. It climbs with you — work, training, surviving. Come back now and again if you care to see it move."

He was already turning back to the ledger, dipping his quill. "That's you in the rolls, Alaric Red, Novice. Board's on the far wall — slips marked with the green band are Novice work. Anything else, you ask a clerk at the counter."

Behind him the door opened and let in the noise of the morning street, two men in mud-spattered leathers coming in talking over each other about the Catacombs road.

messages.mes:
"Burial galleries, then." The clerk took the slip, glanced at the wax seal, and pulled the ledger toward him. "Old Crown Catacombs — you know where the ruined chapel is? Hour west on the west road. There's a stair down under it, and the level one galleries run off it. The wardens keep the entry blessed, so nothing walks up out of there on its own; trouble's all below."

He wrote Alaric's name against the contract, sanded the line, and held the slip out. A small seal at its foot had shifted to read ACTIVE.

"Slip stays with you. When the work's done, bring it back — the seal turns READY once we've word or proof the galleries are cleared. Cull work like this, the wardens count what's put down; they'll confirm it at the chapel. Sixty coppers at this counter when it's done, not from the wardens, mind — the Guild pays, the wardens only confirm."

He closed the ledger. "Anything happen down there — anything strange, anything above your weight — you walk out. Dead Novices don't collect."

One of the mud-spattered men looked over from the board at the word Catacombs, then went back to his arguing.

The slip was thin, the paper stiff, and it sat in Alaric's hand with the faint warmth of the seal.

messages.mes:
The west road was cart-rutted and busy at first — milk carts, a string of pack mules, two women walking with hoes over their shoulders — and thinned the farther he went. Hedgerows gave way to low dry-stone walls, the walls to scrub, and by mid-morning the traffic had shrunk to wheel tracks in dried mud and the creak of grasshoppers.

An hour out, the chapel showed itself across a field of close-cropped grass: a roofless nave, walls of grey stone gone soft-edged with age, one gable still standing with a empty window in it like a dropped jaw. A warden's hut leaned against the south wall, and a thin line of smoke rose from its chimney.

Two men in temple grey sat outside it on a bench, mending a net of some kind between them. A third stood near the chapel door, where the grass stopped short as if mown, and a slab of stone lay tilted in the ground there with an iron ring set in it. The smell of old incense hung around the doorway, faint and bitter.

The one by the door saw Alaric coming and straightened up. Not hostile — just attentive, the way men get at a post where visitors are rare and usually there for the same reason.

"Guild?" he called across the grass. "You'll be for the galleries, then. Show me your slip and I'll not have to ask twice."

The bench pair had stopped mending to watch. A crow called somewhere back along the road. Down under the tilted slab, if the ear was good, there was the kind of silence a hole makes — a whole world of it, waiting on the ring.

messages.mes:
The warden took the slip, turned it toward the light, and thumbed the seal. "ACTIVE, right enough." He handed it back and put two fingers in his mouth; the bench pair looked up. "Come on, then. Ring work's a two-man lift."

It took all three of them. The slab came up groaning on a pivot of packed earth, and a hole opened in the ground — a stair of worn steps dropping into a smell of cold stone and old dust, a little sweet at the edge of it, like incense burned long ago in a shut room. Cold air breathed up out of it against their shins.

"Level one's the upper galleries," the warden said, pointing down the stair with his chin. "Bone shelves along the walls, dead ends, one gallery runs further than the rest — don't take it far, that one goes down to level two and the things down there aren't yours to deal with. Skeletons walk the open floors. Put them down and they stay down for a season or so. Anything you're not sure of—" he shrugged, "—you know what the Guild clerk told you."

The bench pair held the slab up while he went down. Behind him, unhurried, they let it settle back with a boom that travelled away along the stone like a slow wave, and the daylight cut to a bar, to a crack, to nothing. A faint glow lingered in the walls instead — pale markings, worn almost smooth, that gave off light the way old snow does.

The stair ended in a short passage. Niches opened on either side, each one stacked with bones gone dry and grey, skulls facing outward in neat rows. Most of them were still. The floor was swept smooth by decades of feet — warden feet, Guild feet — and a fine grey dust lay over everything, undisturbed except where something had dragged through it in a straight, deliberate line, in and out of the passage ahead.

Down that way, in the dark where the wall-glow thinned, something clicked. Bone on bone, twice, then quiet.

messages.mes:
The passage ran straight for thirty paces, then opened into the first gallery — a long low room, ceiling close enough that the wall-glow reached most of it. Bone niches lined both sides, and between them stood two stone benches worn slick in the middle. The drag-marks in the dust converged here from three directions.

The clicking came from the far end, past a pillar. Not hurried. The unhurried sound of something that had nowhere to be.

Alaric followed it, and around the pillar the source showed itself: a skeleton, man-height, standing half in the thinning glow with one hand braced against the wall. It was doing nothing so grand as prowling — it was running its free hand along the stone, slow sweeps, pausing, sweeping again. Dry sinew creaked at the elbow. Its skull was turned toward the wall, jaw hanging, and the sound had been its finger bones tapping the stone as it went.

It had not turned. Whether it had not noticed him or had nothing left to notice with, there was no telling. Dust sheeted its shoulders. A rusted knife still hung at its hip on a rotted belt, half the blade gone to orange.

The wall-hand kept sweeping. Tap. Pause. Tap.

Past the thing, at the gallery's far end, the passage forked — one way running level into darkness where the glow gave out entirely, the other sloping gently down, and from somewhere down that slope came a second sound: a slow, irregular scraping, like something being dragged a few feet, resting, dragged again.

The first skeleton's finger reached the end of its sweep, paused, and began the pass back the other way.

The lance went from his staff to the thing's back before it finished its sweep — a spear of fire that cracked across the gallery like green wood splitting, struck the dust-sheeted spine dead center, and burst. Flame wrapped the ribcage, the dry bone igniting where it touched, dust flashing to ash in a puff. The skull swung, jaw clacking, and a sound came out of it — a hollow hiss through the vertebrae, nothing a throat could have made.

It did not lunge. It lurched backward, one foot, two, the burning shoulder already guttering out as the flame found nothing left to eat, its elbow joint scorched loose so the arm hung crooked. Its boots — leather gone to stiff brown shell — scraped the swept floor as it retreated the length of a bench, then another pace past it, the rusted knife's sheath catching the wall-glow. It stopped at MEDIUM range, in the thin light near the fork, and stood swaying very slightly, finger bones opening and closing on the hand that still worked.

The dragging sound down the slope had gone quiet.

The gallery held the smell of singed dust and old fat. The skeleton stood between the benches and the fork, skull tilted now toward Alaric, sockets empty of anything at all, and did not come on.

The bolt left his staff as a tight line of pale force, crossed the gallery in a blink, and took the skeleton square in the breastbone. The crack of it went down the whole frame at once — spine, hips, knees — and the thing came apart standing up. Ribs showered the bench behind it. The skull dropped last, bounced once on the swept floor, rolled a half-turn, and lay still with its empty sockets toward the ceiling. Dust hung in the air where it had stood, settling slowly through the wall-glow.

Then the gallery was quiet again. The slope stayed silent; whatever had been dragging itself down there kept its own counsel. The fork waited in its thin light, the level passage running off into black on one side, the downward slope on the other.

A faint warmth at his hip — the pouch, heavier by a handful: a curl of pale, bone-hard hide and a jointed tail-segment, there without his having touched the remains at all.

Something shifted in his chest as the kill settled, a pressure like held water finding level, and he could feel it now plainly: a threshold, crossed. Strength arriving with nowhere to go yet, five loose points of it waiting on his word.

The skeleton's dust finished settling over the benches. Down the stair, far behind, the catacombs gave back nothing but their own cold air.

messages.mes:
The dark passage swallowed the glow within a dozen steps. He kept one hand on the left wall and went by feel, the staff's butt tapping ahead of him, the air growing colder and stiller until his own breathing seemed loud. The wall under his palm changed — niches again, their openings passing under his fingers like empty eye sockets in a row.

The glow came back faintly, then more than faintly, from somewhere ahead: a cold blue seam, sourceless, leaking around a corner where the passage bent. As he neared it the floor gave up its dust. The stones here had been swept too, but lately — drag-marks still sharp-edged in them, dozens of passes, all running toward the bend.

The clicking started again beyond it. Closer now. Two taps, a pause, then a longer chattering rattle like a kettle of loose bones shaken once, and silence. Then footsteps — dry, uneven, many-jointed — coming along the bending passage toward the blue light. Not hurrying.

He had perhaps ten paces of dark passage behind him, the blue seam ahead, and the sound coming on. There was a shallow recess in the right-hand wall where a burial shelf had collapsed into rubble — knee-high, wide enough for a man — and the drag-marks ran straight past it toward the bend, as if whatever swept this floor had never had reason to step off the path.

The footsteps reached the corner. The blue light threw a shadow first — long, wrong-angled, the silhouette of a skull too large at the jaw — and then the thing itself swung into view at the seam's edge, twenty feet off: another skeleton, this one taller and thinner than the wall-hand had been, its ribs bound with loops of greenish copper wire, a second skull tucked under one arm like a loaf. Its eye sockets had pinpoints of the same blue light in them.

The pinpoints fixed on him.

Then it turned and went. Not lurching — hurrying now, joints clicking fast, backward and away down the bending passage, its uneven gait carrying it swiftly toward the far seam of blue light. Before it reached that corner it slipped sideways behind a slab of fallen ceiling leaning against the wall, and its shape broke apart in the shadows: a long shin bone here, the edge of the wired ribcage there, the skull's blue pinpoints burning steady in the gap between stone and wall.

Twenty-some paces off now, half hidden, watching. The pinpoints didn't waver.

The passage held its cold quiet. Drag-marks ran everywhere toward where it hid. Down the slope behind him, far off, the dragging sound had started again — slow, patient, closer than before.

Heat rolled down the passage ahead of him. The lance of fire skimmed low over the drag-marked stones, licked past the edge of the fallen slab, and broke against the hiding frame in a gout of orange. The copper wire flared green, then white. Bone blackened and split with small popping cracks, and the thing came apart where it cowered — ribs collapsing inward, the long shin bone charring where it lay, the skull's blue pinpoints guttering out mid-stare.

Burning wire hissed against stone. Smoke crawled along the ceiling toward the bend, and the second skull on the floor sat untouched in the fire's light, grinning at nothing.

The warmth at his hip again — pelt and tail-segment settling into the pouch without his hands.

The passage dimmed as the flames died to embers among the wreckage. Blue seam-light returned, thin and steady. Behind him, far down the slope, the dragging had stopped. The quiet it left was worse than the sound: the whole dark of the level holding still, listening.

Ahead, past the bend where the skeleton had come from, the blue light widened a little — the seam of a larger space beyond, where the drag-marks all pointed.

messages.mes:
The bend opened into the gallery.

Blue light came from tall niches along both walls, dozens of them, each holding a thin vein of the cold glow behind its burial shelf — enough light to see by, enough shadow to hide in. The chamber ran long and wide, its ceiling propped on stone columns, and the floor told the story plainly: swept bare in the lanes, heaped in the corners, and everywhere marked with those patient drag-lines converging here like ruts in a cart-yard.

Bones lay in those heaps. Not scattered — sorted, or being sorted. Stacks of femurs. Ribs bundled. And skulls, a low row of them along the far wall, maybe twenty, all facing into the room.

Two of the restless ones stood at the heaps mid-way down the gallery, working with slow, deliberate care. One lifted a bundle of bones in both hands and set it on a pile; the other dragged a fallen slab a few inches, then stopped. The dragging sound he'd heard. Its skull turned toward the bend first — and the worker froze with its bundle half-raised, pinpoints of blue in its sockets finding him across thirty feet of swept stone.

They did not rush him. The one with the bundle set it down, unhurried, the way a man sets down his tools. Then both straightened to their full height and stood facing him, still, in the blue-veined dark.

Behind them, at the gallery's far end, the floor sloped down through a wide arch into deeper black — the passage running toward level two that the warden's warning had named. Something down there dragged, once, faintly, and went quiet.

Heat washed the far wall; the skeleton's shoulder burned, then its wired ribcage caught, and the blue pinpoints guttered out as the whole frame sagged against the column, folded, and came apart in a smoking heap of scorched bone.

Its pelt and tail found their way into his pouch before he thought about it, the way the others had.

Silence came back to the gallery. Real silence — no dragging from the slope, no clicking in the corners. The heat of the lance still hung in the cold air, and somewhere overhead a crack ticked through the stone.

The other one remained where it had stood the whole time, at the bone heaps a dozen paces off. It had watched its fellow burn and had not fled, not advanced, not raised a hand. Its pinpoints burned steady on him, and slowly — very slowly — it lowered itself, folding its jointed frame down onto the swept floor, kneeling among the bones it had spent the morning sorting.

It stayed there, hands open on its thighs, looking up at him.

messages.mes:
Fire ran down the gallery one more time and broke over the kneeling thing like a wave over a rock. It never lifted its head. The flames took its bowed neck and shoulders, the bones blackened, and the blue pinpoints dimmed and went out while it held its strange posture — then the whole frame came apart into charred pieces, settling among the bones it had spent its existence arranging.

The heat rolled back against him and faded. His own hands had begun to tremble, a fine, buzzing emptiness spreading up through his arms — the last of his mana gone with that cast, leaving the gallery colder than before.

Something else settled into him alongside the hollowness: a quiet, deepening weight, like a candle flame drawn higher. He had grown stronger, and he knew it the way one knows one's own heartbeat.

A scorched pelt and tail slid into his pouch with the rest.

The gallery lay still. Four heaps of burned bone and wire, the swept floor, the bone heaps along the walls — all of it the work of creatures that had done nothing but sort and drag and dig, and had died for it. The slope down gaped dark at the far end, breathing its cold air up at him, and the fork back toward the upper galleries waited behind.

messages.mes:
He settled against a column near the fork, staff across his knees, and let the quiet have him. Meditation came easier than it had that morning — the emptiness in his arms filled slowly, a cool trickle that pooled and deepened, and the ache behind his eyes loosened. Twice the faint dragging from the slope reached him, far down toward level two, and faded again. He let it go.

Two hours by the feel of the cold. When he rose, his legs were stiff and his mana hummed full, bright and ready behind his breastbone.

The walk back up was uneventful. The passage narrowed, climbed, and opened into the upper burial galleries — the same dim vaults he had walked that morning, dust sheets and slab niches and the low ceiling pressing close. No clicking here. No dragging. The gallery where the sheeted one had come at him lay as he had left it: the fallen sheet, the scattered bones, the dark.

He stood in the hush and listened past it. Farther along the gallery, deeper into the vaults, something ticked — faint, rhythmic, like a nail tapped against stone. Then stopped. Then started again, from a different direction, as though whatever made it had turned and kept working.

The gallery branched ahead into two arched openings, and the sound seemed to sit somewhere between them, or beyond.
